deep_dive_html:
In the specialized landscape of salon leasing, a relocation clause—often termed a "Substitution Clause"—is a latent liability that can dismantle a profitable enterprise. Landlords frequently utilize these provisions to reposition high-performing tenants to inferior, low-visibility units to accommodate larger, higher-rent anchor tenants. While the lease may deceptively state the new space will be "comparable" in size and utility, the technical reality for a salon is far more complex. A salon is not a generic retail footprint; it is a highly engineered environment dependent on specific plumbing, heavy-duty electrical loads for dryers, and specialized ventilation systems.

The trap lies in the landlord's ability to move you to a space that lacks the necessary infrastructure, effectively forcing you to absorb massive capital expenditures for reconfiguration. Without specific language, you may find yourself responsible for the costs of rerouting drainage, upgrading electrical panels, or installing new HVAC ductwork, all while your revenue plummets during the transition period.

The Standard for Tenant Protection

To neutralize this threat, an elite lease negotiation must move beyond mere "comparability" and focus on "functional equivalence" and "cost indemnity." A market-standard protection includes a comprehensive "Make-Good" provision. This requires the landlord to bear the entirety of the costs associated with the move, including all plumbing, electrical, and HVAC modifications required to replicate your existing build-out to its original standard.

Furthermore, a sophisticated tenant must negotiate for the following protections:

  • Full reimbursement of all construction, permitting, and professional fees associated with the relocation.
  • Mandatory compensation for business interruption, including lost revenue and the cost of temporary relocation.
  • A "Right of Refusal" regarding the new space's suitability for salon-specific operations and visibility.
  • A "No-Relocation" period, typically prohibiting any move during the first 36 to 60 months of the lease term.
  • Requirement for the landlord to maintain the same level of foot traffic and signage visibility.

title: Landlord Tricks in Relocation Clauses for Salons
